t:
Back-formed from the accusative diem (at a time when the vowel was still long), from Proto-Italic *djēm, the accusative of *djous, from Proto-Indo-European *dyḗws (“heaven, sky”). The original nominative survives as *diūs in two fossilised phrases: mē diūs fidius (an interjection) and nū diūs tertius (“day before yesterday”, literally “now (is) the third day”). The d in diēs is a puzzle with some suggesting dialect borrowing and others referring to an etymon *diyew- via Lindeman's Law. But note the possible Proto-Italic allophony between *-CjV- and *-CiV-, which may be the cause for this divergence (See WT:AITC).
Cognate with Ancient Greek Ζήν (Zḗn), Old Armenian տիւ (tiw, “daytime”), Old Irish día, Welsh dydd, Polish dzień, but not English day, which is a false cognate. The Italic stem was also the source of Iovis, the genitive of Iuppiter and was generally interchangeable with it in earlier times, still shown by the analogical formation Diēspiter.
Derived from Etruscan. Etruscan names of stops were the stop followed by /eː/.
g: The name of the letter C.

t: From Proto-Italic *kəntom, from Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm. Formal cognates include Sanskrit श॒त (śatá), Old Church Slavonic съто (sŭto), and Old English hund (whence English hundred, with an attached suffix). Doublet of *suta.

From Proto-Italic *karō, from Proto-Indo-European *(s)ker-. Cognate with Dutch scheren, German scheren, Danish skære, Norwegian skjære, Swedish skära; and (from Indo-European) with Ancient Greek κείρω (keírō, “to cut off”), English shear, Albanian harr (“to cut, to mow”), Lithuanian ski̇̀rti (“to separate”), Welsh ysgar (“separate”). See also sharp.

Etymology tree

Proto-Italic *tersā
Latin terra
Inherited from Proto-Italic *tersā, from Proto-Indo-European *ters-eh₂ (“dry land”), from *ters- (“dry”). Doublet of torreō. Cognate with Ancient Greek τέρσομαι (térsomai), Old Irish tír, Sanskrit तृषा (tṛ́ṣā), Old English þurst (whence English thirst). Compare the semantics of Ancient Greek χέρσος (khérsos).
g: dry land (as opposed to watery parts of the Earth)
ground, floor (the surface of the land)

t: From Proto-Italic *apweriō (alternatively reconstructed as Proto-Italic *apwerjō) from Proto-Indo-European *h₂epó (“off, from”) (whence ab) + *h₂wer- (“to cover, shut”) + *-ye-. Cognate with Sanskrit अपिवृणोति (apivṛṇoti, “to close, cover”), Oscan veru (“door”, pl.), Ancient Greek ἀείρω (aeírō, “to lift, raise”), Lithuanian atvérti (“to open”), Proto-Slavic *ot(ъ)verti (“to open”), and Old Armenian գեր (ger, “above, hyper-”). Related to operiō (“to cover”).
g: to uncover, make or lay bare, reveal, clear
to make visible, discover, show, reveal, lay open

t:
From Old Latin olle (“he, that”) (also ollus, olla), from Proto-Italic *olnos, from Proto-Indo-European *h₂ol-no-s or *h₂l̥-no-s, from *h₂el- (“beyond, other”). Cognate with Latin uls (“beyond”), alius (“other”), and alter (“the other”); Umbrian ulu (“to that place”), Old Church Slavonic лани (lani, “last year”, literally “in that (year)”).
Initial i- from o- has no parallel case and owe to contamination from is and iste, or the palatalizing effect of l exilis.

From Proto-Italic *fundos, from Proto-Indo-European *bʰudʰ-(m)n-o-s, thematized from *bʰudʰmḗn (“bottom”). Compare the similar treatment in Ancient Greek πύνδαξ (púndax, “bottom”). Cognates include Sanskrit बुध्न (budhna), Persian بن (bon, “root, bottom”), Ancient Greek πυθμήν (puthmḗn, “bottom”), and Old English botm (modern bottom).
g: farm, piece of land, estate, demesne

Etymology tree
Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰew-
Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰewd-
Proto-Indo-European *-né-
Proto-Indo-European *-ti
Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰunédti
Proto-Italic *hundō
Latin fundō
From Proto-Italic *hundō, from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰu-né-d-ti ~ *ǵʰu-n-d-énti, nasal infix present of the root *ǵʰew-d- (“to pour”), extended from *ǵʰew-. The change from Proto-Italic *h- to Latin f- is unique to this word; Weiss takes it as regular before *-u-. The perfect form fūdī is potentially the continuation of a PIE root aorist *ǵʰéwd-t ~ *ǵʰud-ént. The perfect participle fūsus could continue an earlier participle *ǵʰud-tós. Cognates include Ancient Greek χέω (khéō) and Gothic 𐌲𐌹𐌿𐍄𐌰𐌽 (giutan).
g: to melt, cast, found, make by smelting

t: Seemingly from fundō, -ere + -ō. Perhaps remodeled by analogy with Oscan first conjugation perfect subjunctives marked by the sequence -tt-i-.
From moveō + -bilis. Developed from *moubilis, from Proto-Italic *moweðlis, with the diphthong ou monophthongizing to long ō.
